finalText:
Same starting point and ending point, different history.

Merge adds a new commit that ties both branches together, keeping all the old commits exactly as they happened. Rebase instead picks up your branch's commits and replants them on top of the other branch, one by one, as if you'd started there — so history ends up as one straight line, no merge commit, no fork.

That trade shows up in two ways:

- **History shape.** Merge keeps the true, branchy story of what happened. Rebase rewrites it into a clean, straight line.
- **Safety on shared branches.** Rebase changes commit history, so if anyone else already has the old commits, their copy and yours will clash. Never rebase a branch other people are pulling from.

Rough rule of thumb:

- **Merging in main, or any shared branch** → merge. Keeps history honest and doesn't break anyone else's copy.
- **Your own branch, before you've shared it** → rebase. Cleans up your commits into a tidy line before it joins main.
